                                          "Sarah M., Top Producer in Austin, TX"

                                          "Jennifer K., Miami Real Estate Agent"
  plus "Mike R." on /instagram-bio-for-realtors and "David K." on
  /features/analytics.
The clincher: "Sarah M." is simultaneously a Luxury Agent in Austin TX, a Top
Producer in Austin TX, and from Beverly Hills. Same initials, three different
biographies. These were not left in place out of doubt about what they are —
they sit outside US-156's scope and removing marketing copy across six more

### US-157 — structured data — 2026-09-08 — PASSES

The story described 3 Product-snippet impressions and asked for deliberate
coverage. What the audit actually found was that the site was publishing false
claims to search, and had been since before US-111.

INVENTED STAR RATINGS ON 31 PAGES. Every one carried
`aggregateRating: {ratingValue: "4.8", reviewCount: "523"}`. US-111 had already
identified this exact pair as "both invented", removed it from the landing page,
and left a comment saying why — but missed five other sources that were still
emitting it: seo.ts (three separate literals), PageSEO.tsx, and
SEO_CONFIG.ratings, which fed all 23 city pages through LocationTemplate. Google
renders stars in search results from this field, so the site was showing a
fabricated 4.8-from-523-reviews to everyone who searched. AggregateRating count
in the built output: 31 before, 0 after.

The genuinely data-driven ones were kept. FullProfilePage and ReviewSchema
compute ratings from the `testimonials` table — real reviews of a real agent —
and are untouched. generateSoftwareApplicationSchema was emitting an
aggregateRating with `undefined` values because SchemaMarkup calls it without
ratings; it is now conditional, so absent rather than malformed.

A FALSE PRICE FOR A NAMED PLAN. The literal '39' appeared in five places, and
seo.config.ts:230 attached it to a node explicitly named "Professional" —
which costs 49. The homepage's SoftwareApplication Offer also published price
'39'. There is no $39 plan; the matrix is 0, 29, 49, 99, 299. This is the same
phantom figure US-156 found on /vs/linktree, which suggests it was once a real
price and nothing propagated the change. Every occurrence now derives from
PRICING_PLANS. The homepage's single Offer became an AggregateOffer with
lowPrice 29 / highPrice 299, which is the honest shape for a tiered product.
Verified in the built output: the only offer values now are 0, 29 and 29-299.

EIGHTEEN FAQ QUESTIONS MARKED UP BUT NOT ON THE PAGE, across six pages —
/vs/linktree, /vs/beacons, /for-real-estate-agents, /instagram-bio-for-realtors
and both free tools. FAQPage schema describing content a visitor cannot see is a
structured-data policy violation and a manual-action risk. Rather than delete
the markup, the answers were already written, so they are now rendered:
src/components/seo/FaqSection.tsx takes one array per page and produces both the
JSON-LD (faqPageSchema) and the visible <details> list. They cannot drift,
because they are the same array. Confirmed in the built HTML that the questions
appear in the rendered text with the <script> content stripped out.

BreadcrumbList was missing from /vs/linktree, /vs/beacons and /vs/later while
/features/*, /for/* and the tools all had one. Added; 52 -> 55 in the output.
/features/analytics has no '@graph' schema block at all, so it was left alone
rather than restructured — noted here rather than half-done.

The check that keeps all of this true: scripts/lib/seo-audit.mjs now parses
every JSON-LD block in the built HTML and fails on unparseable JSON, on the
4.8/523 pair specifically, on an aggregateRating missing ratingValue or
reviewCount, and on a FAQPage question absent from the rendered text. Proven
against the real build rather than asserted — a malformed block, a reinstated
4.8/523, and an invented FAQ question ("Does AgentBio secretly cure baldness
overnight?") each failed it with the right message, and the restored build
passes.

That last check had a bug worth recording. The first version stripped HTML tags
but not <script> CONTENT, so a FAQ question trivially "appeared on the page" by
matching its own JSON-LD source, and the baldness question passed. Fixing it
immediately surfaced all 18 real cases. A check that cannot fail is worse than
no check, and this one could not fail until it was tested against something that
should fail.

No Review or aggregateRating schema was added anywhere. Seven hardcoded,
unverifiable testimonials are still live elsewhere on the site (listed under the
US-156 entry); emitting review markup from them would have converted a content
problem into a structured-data misrepresentation.

Verification: build exits 0 (51 routes), verify:seo passes all 51 with the new
structured-data rules, tsc --noEmit clean, impeccable clean on FaqSection.

Test suite: 632 passed / 13 failed at 90s — the load-flaky pattern again, and I
checked it properly this time because a lot of pages changed. Run as a group of
seven, eight failed; run ONE AT A TIME, every single one passed: SubmitReview
5/5, Settings 6/6, LeadDetailModal 7/7, Register 3/3, ContactForm 3/3.
routes.test.ts passed in both the group and alone. The stable floor remains
repo-hygiene x2, analytics and analyticsEvents.

### US-158 — link acquisition programme — 2026-09-08 — PASSES

The artefacts are built. NOBODY HAS BEEN CONTACTED, no account was created, no
listing was submitted, and no placement exists. That half is a person's and is
written up as such.

THE RESEARCH CHANGED THE PLAN. Searching "best link in bio tools for real estate
agents 2026" on 2026-09-08 returned a first page dominated by COMPETITOR-OWNED
content marketing, not neutral roundups — linqin.in, simplelistings.co,
direct.me (twice), clientkeepercrm.com and linkship.cc are all competing
products marketing themselves. A competitor will not add us to their roundup,
and pitching them only tells them we exist. That SERP is won by publishing a
better page than theirs, which is what US-155 and US-156 started, not by
outreach.

The real targets are one step out, and every URL in Tier 1 was actually
retrieved rather than guessed: HousingWire's marketing-tools, software and
AI-tools roundups; The Close's software and apps roundups; Inman's AI-tools
piece. Tier 2 (G2, Capterra/GetApp/Software Advice, Product Hunt) and Tier 3
(r/realtors, agent Facebook groups, brokerages, state associations) are listed
as CATEGORIES and the doc says plainly that their submission routes were NOT
opened or verified — treating an unverified link as checked is how a target list
becomes fiction. No contact names or email addresses are listed, because I
verified none and a wrong name is worse than no name.

/press ships, prerendered, in the sitemap, linked from the footer so it is not
orphaned the way the comparison pages were. Every claim is checkable: what the
product does (five capabilities, each linking to its feature page), who it is
for, and what it costs — with the price table read from PRICING_PLANS so it
cannot drift from the checkout. Verified in the built HTML that it carries $0,
$29, $49, $99 and $299 and NONE of 4.8, 523, "2,000+", $39 or $19. No customer
counts, no funding, no awards, no press mentions, no ratings, no testimonials.
The page says so where a reader would expect one.

Product screenshots are deliberately absent. Real ones need a populated account
and a person to choose what to show; generating something representative would
mean inventing an agent's listings, which is the same failure as the fabricated
testimonials. The page asks the reader to request current ones instead.

Three sendable templates in docs/seo/OUTREACH_TEMPLATES.md — roundup author,
directory submission, partnership. They carry no invented social proof, they
name the specific article, they say out loud where a competitor is the better
choice, and there is no follow-up sequence. The directory template tells the
sender to check the price against /pricing rather than typing it from memory,
because typing it from memory is exactly how $39 ended up in six places
describing a plan that does not exist.

docs/seo/SEO_RECOVERY_CHECKLIST.md is the single owner-facing page: what eleven
stories changed, and the seven things only a person can do, ordered by damage.
Removing the seven remaining fabricated testimonials is first, and the link
document says explicitly not to pitch HousingWire until it is done — a reviewer
who checks one quoted agent and finds nothing will not check the second.

A REAL REGRESSION, CAUGHT BY CHECKING IN ISOLATION. routes.test.ts began failing
after the press page was added, and unlike every other suspect this batch it
failed ALONE, not only under load. The page links six logo files (/logo.png,
/Cover.webp and so on) and the test's link scanner measured them against the
route table, reporting each as a link to a non-existent route. They are static
assets in public/ that React Router never sees. Fixed in the test rather than in
the page — it now skips paths with a file extension, the same rule
isReservedSegment already uses in functions/_lib/social-meta.ts. Confirmed the
check still has teeth by pointing a link at /this-route-does-not-exist: it
failed, and passed again once restored.

Verification: build exits 0 (52 routes), verify:seo passes all 52, tsc --noEmit
clean, impeccable clean on Press.tsx. The full suite gave 20 failures at 103s —
the worst run of the batch and also its slowest — but run in isolation the four
files give exactly the four stable pre-existing failures (repo-hygiene x2,
analytics, analyticsEvents) and routes.test.ts passes 3/3.

### US-159 — remove every fabricated claim — 2026-09-08 — PASSES

Authorised by Dj: "No fabricated text, we need to remove false claims and false
testimonies." This is the third pass at the same defect, and the first one that
swept the whole of src/ rather than the pages a story happened to touch.

WHAT THE SWEEP FOUND, beyond the seven testimonials already flagged:

  Five different invented agent counts, plus the original still live:
    2,847        instagram-bio-analyzer capture modal (twice)
    4,200+       listing-description-generator modal and page (four places)
    2,000+       /vs/beacons and /vs/linktree
    3,000+       /vs/later
    10,000+      /tools/instagram-bio-analyzer
    5,000+       /for-real-estate-agents and /instagram-bio-for-realtors
  US-111 documented "2,500+ vs 5,000+ on two pages one click apart" as the
  original defect. 5,000+ was still on two landing pages, untouched, and four
  more numbers had been added since.

  Hardcoded ratings: "4.9/5 rating" in both capture modals, and a
  "4.9/5 Agent Rating" stat tile on the analyzer page.

  "Used by agents at Keller Williams, Coldwell Banker, RE/MAX" — three real
  firms named as customers. A claim about them as much as about us.

  Four stat tiles on /tools/instagram-bio-analyzer: "2,847+ Agents Analyzed",
  "3X Average Lead Increase", "$50M+ In Deals Generated", "4.9/5 Agent Rating".
  Replaced with four things the tool actually does — 5 scored categories, 3
  rewrites, free, ~60s.

  Eight more named testimonials: three on the listing-description-generator
  page, one in each capture modal, and two whole fabricated sections —
  "Success Stories from {city} Agents" in LocationTemplate, which rendered two
  fictional agents with "3 closings", "15 leads/month", "$2M+ in sales" and
  "10x engagement" on ALL 26 city pages, each claiming to be local; and a
  four-testimonial "Agent Success Stories" block on /vs/later.

  And the worst of it, because it goes to real inboxes: the Instagram bio
  analyzer email drip quoted invented percentile benchmarks ("Average Agent:
  ~7 leads/month", "Top Performer: ~45 leads/month"), a section headed "Real
  results from ${market} agents" listing "Agent A: 3 -> 18 leads/month (6X)"
  and "Agent B: 8 -> 31 (4X)", "10,000+ real estate professionals trust us",
  "Average user generates 15+ leads/month" and "847 agents closed deals from
  AgentBio leads last month alone". All removed; the surrounding copy was
  rewritten to make the same point without inventing numbers.

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY KEPT, with the reason recorded in the new test's
ALLOWED_FILES so the next sweep does not re-litigate it:
  - BioAnalyzerForm's "0 / 1-3 / 4-10 / 10+ leads/month" dropdown — it asks the
    visitor about their own current situation. Not a claim.
  - "Keller Williams, Coldwell Banker, etc." as the placeholder in a "your
    brokerage" input. An example of what to type.
  - features/Testimonials' "Star display (4.8/5.0, 4.9/5.0, etc.)" — product
    documentation for the testimonial widget, listed beside "Automatically
    updates as you add reviews".
  - The ExampleBio demos and bio-generator's suggested credentials
    ("$50M+ in luxury sales") — illustrations of what an agent might write about
    themselves, not claims about us.
  - Zapier's own published "5,000+ apps" figure in the integration modal.
  - ReviewSchema and FullProfilePage's aggregateRating, computed from the real
    `testimonials` table.
Nothing was reworded into a vaguer version of the same claim. A claim either had
something behind it or it went.

THE GUARD. src/marketing-claims.test.ts fails the build on any of five shapes:
a hardcoded named testimonial, a customer count, a star rating, an outcome
metric, or another company named as a customer. Three cleanups in a row each
believed themselves thorough and each missed instances, because the copy lives
in a dozen files and nothing compared them.

It has two tests, and the second one matters: "is actually able to fail" asserts
that the five rules still match the exact strings removed in US-111, US-156,
US-157 and US-159. A guard that silently stops matching is worse than none.
Demonstrated for real as well — injecting "Join 5,000+ agents - 4.9/5 rating"
into Pricing.tsx produced two findings and a failure, and removing it passed.

One bug in the guard, worth recording. The first version checked whether each
LINE looked like a comment, which flagged the middle lines of every multi-line
removal note — the notes quote the claim they deleted, which is the point of
them — and made the test unfixable without deleting the explanations. It now
tracks block state across lines.

Verification: build exits 0 (52 routes), verify:seo passes all 52, tsc --noEmit
clean. Checked the BUILT output too, not just source: a 248-file scan of dist/
for 24 banned strings returns only coincidental matches — "523" inside the award
icon's SVG path data and inside export-vendor's MD5 constants — plus the
legitimate feature description and the real computed ratings.

Full suite 624 passed / 23 failed at 127s, the heaviest-loaded run of the whole
session. Every suspect passes alone: marketing-claims 2/2, routes 3/3,
ContactForm 3/3, Register 3/3, Settings 6/6, SubmitReview 5/5, LeadDetailModal
7/7. The stable floor is unchanged — repo-hygiene x2, analytics, analyticsEvents.

## Platform Improvement Loop — 2026-09-09 (self-paced, 15 iterations)

### Iteration 1/15 — US-160: 17 MB of source maps were being published to the CDN

vite.config.ts carried `sourcemap: 'hidden'` with the comment "These are hidden
source maps that won't expose source code to users". That comment is wrong, and
it had been wrong long enough to survive US-125, which was explicitly about the
17 MB of maps in the build output and only reduced them.

`hidden` omits the `//# sourceMappingURL=` comment from the emitted bundle. That
stops a *browser* fetching the map on its own. It does not stop anyone else: the
map filename is the chunk filename plus `.map`, and the chunk filename is in the
network tab of every visit. `https://agentbio.net/assets/index-<hash>.js.map`
returned the whole TypeScript source — 193 files, 17 MB, 71% of a 24 MB deploy.
Every query shape, every RLS assumption, every route not yet announced.

The justification recorded in the comment was Sentry symbolication. Nothing
consumed them. There is no @sentry/vite-plugin, no `sentry-cli sourcemaps`
invocation, and no upload step anywhere in .github/workflows — `@sentry/react`
is the only Sentry dependency and it needs the maps on Sentry's side, not on
Cloudflare's. They were cost with no benefit attached.

WHAT CHANGED
  - vite.config.ts: `sourcemap: BUILD_SOURCEMAPS ? 'hidden' : false`, off by
    default. The comment now says what 'hidden' actually does.
  - The flag is a real escape hatch, not a formality: `BUILD_SOURCEMAPS=true`
    is what a local `npm run analyze` wants, and what a future CI job would set
    to upload to an error tracker and then delete dist/**/*.map before deploy.
  - scripts/check-bundle-size.mjs — already the CI `size-check` job — now fails
    if any .map reaches dist/assets without that flag. The check runs before the
    per-chunk budget loop so it reports even when a chunk is also over budget.

VERIFICATION, against real builds rather than reasoning about the flag:
  - default build: dist 24 MB -> 6.4 MB, `ls dist/assets/*.map` = 0.
  - `BUILD_SOURCEMAPS=true npx vite build`: 193 maps, as before.
  - the guard was demonstrated failing, not just written: dropping one .map into
    dist/assets produced the failure and its message, and removing it passed.
  - tsc --noEmit clean.

NOTED, NOT FIXED — `npm run size-check` is already red on main, and was before
this change: export-vendor is 605.0 KB against a 600 KB vendor budget (jspdf +
html2canvas). Same chunk hash before and after, so it is untouched by this work.
A CI gate that is red by default teaches everyone to ignore it, so this is the
candidate for the next iteration.

STORIES OPENED
  - US-161: `npx impeccable detect src` reports 65 AI-generated-design tells —
    49 ai-color-palette (purple/violet gradients), 10 gradient-text on headings,
    3 side-tab, 1 overused-font, 1 gray-on-color, 1 border-accent-on-rounded.
    CLAUDE.md names every one of these as a default to refuse. Not a lint fix:
    removing a purple gradient means deciding what replaces it, so it needs a
    palette and type decision taken first and then a page-by-page pass. Deferred
    to a later iteration deliberately, per the loop's own rule about work that
    does not fit in one.

### Iteration 2/15 — US-162: the Leads page loaded a PDF library to render a CSV button

Iteration 1 left `npm run size-check` red on main: export-vendor 605 KB against a
600 KB vendor budget. The obvious move is to raise the budget or add an
exception. Both would have been wrong, because the chunk was not lazy.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG. src/lib/exportUtils.ts opened with
`import { jsPDF } from 'jspdf'`. That module also exports exportToCSV, which is
a string builder and a Blob download and touches nothing from jspdf. But a
top-level import makes the jspdf chunk a static dependency of every consumer,
and Rollup cannot tree-shake it away because generatePDFReport in the same
module genuinely uses it.

src/pages/dashboard/Leads.tsx imports exportToCSV and nothing else from there.
Read out of the built output rather than reasoned about:
  Leads-CcCFikjE.js -> exportUtils-RdteEteH.js (3 KB) -> export-vendor (605 KB,
  184 KB gzip)
605 KB on the critical path of the most-visited page in a lead-generation CRM,
for a button that never calls it.

TWO MORE DEFECTS FELL OUT OF THE SAME manualChunks LINE:
  'export-vendor': ['jspdf', 'jspdf-autotable', 'html2canvas']
  - html2canvas is not a dependency of this project. It is not in package.json.
    jspdf references it optionally; the entry did nothing.
  - Naming jspdf there made Rollup place Vite's `__vitePreload` helper inside
    the resulting chunk, so consumers emitted `import{_}from"./export-vendor"` —
    a static import of 605 KB to obtain a 200-byte function.

THE FIX
  - exportUtils.ts loads jsPDF and jspdf-autotable with
    `await Promise.all([import('jspdf'), import('jspdf-autotable')])` inside
    generatePDFReport. exportToPDF and generatePDFReport are now async.
  - Both call sites await them. SearchAnalyticsDashboard's handler is async with
    a try/catch, so the toast follows the download instead of racing it and a
    failed chunk fetch is reported instead of becoming an unhandled rejection;
    ReportBuilder was already inside an async try/catch and just needed the
    await.
  - The manualChunks entry is deleted, not edited. A dynamically imported
    dependency does not need one — Rollup already splits it — and the entry was
    what dragged the preload helper in.

RESULT, from the build: export-vendor no longer exists. jspdf is a 386 KB async
chunk plus a 31 KB autotable chunk, fetched on click. The Leads chunk's static
imports contain no jspdf. exportUtils emits `import("./jspdf.es.min-*.js")`.
`npm run size-check` passes — 195 chunks, one documented exception.

THE TEST TOLD ME SOMETHING I WOULD HAVE MISSED. Making the functions async
without awaiting them at the call sites left `savedFilenames` empty and wrote
two real PDFs into the repository root — the exact US-121 defect the mock exists
to prevent, resurrected by an unawaited promise racing the test's teardown. The
suite caught it in the intermediate state. Both files were deleted; a clean run
now leaves the working tree clean.

The four PDF tests are awaited, and there is a new guard: two tests read
exportUtils.ts as text and assert no top-level import of jspdf or
jspdf-autotable, and that the dynamic form is present. One line restores this
regression, and nothing else in the suite would notice — the page still works,
it just costs half a megabyte to open. 10/10 pass. tsc --noEmit clean.

STORY OPENED — US-163, and it is worse than the one just fixed. The preload
helper has no home of its own, so with export-vendor gone Rollup moved it into
three-vendor (800 KB). FullProfilePage now emits
`import{_}from"./three-vendor-BHOYcAMp.js"` — a static import. That is
/:username, the page every agent puts in their Instagram bio, paying 800 KB /
220 KB gzip for Three.js before first paint whether or not the theme renders a
3D background. Before this iteration the helper was in the jspdf chunk and the
same page paid 605 KB for that, so it has been true continuously and only the
victim changed. It also makes check-bundle-size.mjs's exception text — "lazy-
loaded only on 3D hero sections, never on first paint" — false.

Attempted and reverted: adding 'vite/preload-helper' to the react-vendor array.
The object form of manualChunks resolves entries as package specifiers and the
build dies with `Missing "./preload-helper" specifier in "vite" package`. The
route is the function form of manualChunks, matching the virtual module id,
which means re-deriving every existing grouping by path and proving no chunk
reshuffles. Next iteration.

### Iteration 3/15 — US-163: Three.js was on the critical path of every page

Opened at the end of iteration 2 believing FullProfilePage was the victim.
Writing the guard showed it was worse than that.

THE MECHANISM. Vite's `__vitePreload` helper is a virtual module with no home of
its own, so Rollup files it into whichever manualChunks group it picks. It had
landed in three-vendor. Every chunk that lazy-loads anything then emitted
`import{_}from"./three-vendor-<hash>.js"` — a STATIC import of an 800 KB chunk to
obtain a 200-byte function.

THE ACTUAL BLAST RADIUS, from the guard run against the old config:
  FullProfilePage-B8_AhUTY.js  statically imports three-vendor (800 KB)
  exportUtils-D862ke8l.js      statically imports three-vendor (800 KB)
  index-PBqFv9Am.js            statically imports three-vendor (800 KB)
  jspdf.es.min-Ad-4HYgU.js     statically imports three-vendor (800 KB)
`index-*.js` is the ENTRY. It loads on every route. So every visitor to every
page on the platform — the marketing landing page, the blog, every agent's
public profile — downloaded 800 KB / 220 KB gzip of Three.js before first paint,
whether or not anything on the page rendered 3D. Before US-162 the helper lived
in the jspdf chunk and the same importers paid 605 KB for that instead. This has
been true continuously; only the victim changed.

THE FIX. manualChunks converted from the object form to a function. That is
forced, not stylistic: the object form resolves its entries as package
specifiers, so a virtual module cannot be named in it — putting
`'vite/preload-helper'` in the react-vendor array kills the build with
`Missing "./preload-helper" specifier in "vite" package` (tried in iteration 2,
reverted). A function can match the id directly, and does, first thing.

The groupings moved into a VENDOR_CHUNKS table matched on the package directory
a module resolves into. One deliberate difference from the object form: a
package's transitive dependencies are no longer welded into its group —
recharts' d3-* packages get their own chunks. That could have reshuffled
everything, so it was checked rather than assumed.

VERIFICATION, all against real builds:
  - helper now in react-vendor: `import{_}from"./react-vendor-DtYTAvso.js"`.
  - the only static importers of three-vendor are FloatingGeometry, GradientMesh
    and ThreeDBackground — the 3D components themselves.
  - FullProfilePage's static vendor deps: animation, form, react, state. No three.
  - the entry chunk's: charts, form, react, state, supabase, ui. No three.
  - chunk name set identical before and after — 195 both times, `diff` clean.
  - vendor sizes within 6 KB (react-vendor 155 -> 161.5 KB, the helper and
    react-router; three-vendor 818 -> 797 KB).
  - tsc --noEmit clean; vitest still resolves the config.

THE GUARD, and why the old one could not have caught this. The exception in
check-bundle-size.mjs said three-vendor was "lazy-loaded only on 3D hero
sections, never on first paint". That was false for months and nothing noticed,
because an exception made of prose asserts nothing. It now carries a
`staticImporters` list — the only chunks allowed to `import ... from` it — and
the check walks every built chunk and fails on any other static importer. A
static import renders as `from"./chunk.js"` and a dynamic one as
`import("./chunk.js")`, so matching on `from` picks up exactly the imports that
put a chunk on a critical path.

Demonstrated, not assumed: stashing the new vite.config, rebuilding with the old
one and running the check produced the four-importer failure quoted above.
Restored, it passes.

STORY OPENED — US-164. With three-vendor gone from the entry, what remains
static there is charts-vendor: 394 KB of recharts, in a chunk whose own comment
reads "Charts - dashboard only", loaded on every route including the marketing
landing page. Next iteration.

### Iteration 4/15 — US-164: the landing page shipped recharts to supply clsx

Left over from iteration 3: with three-vendor off the critical path, the entry
chunk still statically imported charts-vendor — 394 KB of recharts, in a chunk
whose own comment in vite.config.ts reads "Charts - dashboard only". The entry
loads on every route, so every visitor to the marketing landing page, every blog
reader and every public profile visitor paid for it.

It was not a stray chart component. All six recharts importers are admin or
dashboard files and all are correctly lazy. The entry pulled exactly ONE binding:

  import{e as Tr}from"./charts-vendor-DgQnpdXW.js"
  ...
  function X(...t){return el(Tr(t))}

`el(Tr(t))` is `twMerge(clsx(inputs))` — cn() from src/lib/utils.ts, which every
component in the app calls. clsx had no assigned home in VENDOR_CHUNKS, recharts
happens to depend on it, so Rollup filed it into charts-vendor and the entry
imported the whole 394 KB chunk to get a 500-byte function.

@babel/runtime's helpers had been adopted the same way. That is why three-vendor
statically imported charts-vendor: `import{_ as xa}` there is `_extends`, and
both recharts and @react-three/drei depend on @babel/runtime. Loading a 3D
profile theme pulled in a charting library to get Object.assign.

This is US-163's defect one layer down, and the generalisation is worth stating:
a tiny shared module with no assigned home gets adopted by whichever large chunk
happens to want it, and every consumer then pays for the whole thing. It is
invisible in a chunk listing — every size looks fine — and shows up only in who
imports what.

THE FIX. clsx, tailwind-merge, class-variance-authority and @babel/runtime named
in VENDOR_CHUNKS, landing in react-vendor, which every page loads anyway.

VERIFICATION:
  - entry static vendor imports: form, react, state, supabase, ui. No charts.
  - charts-vendor's static importers: Analytics, HealthDashboard, SEOManager,
    SearchAnalyticsDashboard. Dashboard and admin only.
  - three-vendor no longer imports charts-vendor.
  - react-vendor 161.5 -> 184.3 KB: four utility packages moving into a chunk
    that was already loaded, against 394 KB leaving the critical path.
  - chunk name set identical to iteration 3's; tsc clean; tests pass.

THE GUARD, generalised. US-163 added a staticImporters list to the over-budget
exception for three-vendor. charts-vendor is under budget, so it was not covered
— the enforcement was tied to the wrong thing. It is now a separate MUST_STAY_LAZY
map keyed by chunk, independent of size, covering three-vendor and charts-vendor.
Its failure message names the actual cause, because "X statically imports Y" does
not tell you what to do about it: look for a tiny shared module with no home and
name it in VENDOR_CHUNKS.

Demonstrated against the pre-fix config, not assumed:
  index-DyYjmFjj.js       statically imports charts-vendor (393.9 KB)
  three-vendor-9DsfYJow.js statically imports charts-vendor (393.9 KB)

Also removed a duplicated block in check-bundle-size.mjs — the budget loop and
its reporting appeared twice, the second copy dead. Introduced by an earlier
edit in this session, caught by node refusing to parse `const violations`
declared twice.

RUNNING TOTAL for a first-time visitor to any public page, across iterations
1-4: 17 MB of source maps off the deploy, 800 KB of Three.js and 394 KB of
recharts off the critical path.

================================================================================
ITERATION 1 (new loop) — US-165: live production credentials in a public repo
================================================================================

WHAT I WAS LOOKING FOR: one thing to make the platform better. I started, as
usual, by establishing a baseline — and the baseline was red. `npm run test:run`
on main: 2 failed, 647 passed.

The failing file was src/repo-hygiene.test.ts, the guard US-121 wrote to hold
the repository root to six markdown files and no loose scripts. Ten files had
been added to the root on 2026-09-04. On its face this is housekeeping.

It was not housekeeping.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY IN THEM:

  SUPABASE_KEYS_GUIDE.md          this deployment's live anon AND service_role
                                  JWTs, in full, under the heading
                                  "These are valid and working! ✅"
  deploy-migrations-ssh.ps1       the root SSH password for the production host,
                                  plus the Postgres superuser password
  migrate-to-coolify.ps1          the Postgres superuser password
  migrate-via-files.ps1           the Postgres superuser password
  test-db-connection.ps1          the Postgres superuser password
  SSH_MIGRATION_GUIDE.md          the Postgres superuser password, four times

And the repository is PUBLIC — confirmed against the GitHub API, not assumed:
`"private": false, "visibility": "public"`. These were world-readable for five
days.

The service_role key is the worst of it. It bypasses every RLS policy in the
database — every row of `leads` and `profiles` included — and it is not
independently revocable: the only way to invalidate it is to rotate JWT_SECRET
and reissue both keys. Its exp is the year 2125, so it was never going to expire
its way out of the problem.

WHY IT SAT THERE FOR FIVE DAYS. The guard worked. It went red the day the files
landed, CI runs `npm run test:coverage`, and so the Test job on main has been
failing since 2026-09-04 — everything merged since merged over a red CI. What
failed was not the detection but the framing: a guard that says "these belong
under docs/" reads like a lint nit, so it got treated as one. Nothing in the
repository was in a position to say "there is a superuser password in that file."

That is the generalisation worth keeping: a guard is only worth what the
attention paid to it is worth, and a guard that understates its own stake
teaches people to scroll past it.

THE FIX, in two halves.

Half one, the purge:
  - deleted the five one-shot migration scripts. The Coolify migration is
    complete (docs/deploy/MIGRATION_COMPLETE.md), nothing in src/ or scripts/
    references them, and every one of them carried a password. Same defect
    US-122 fixed for edge-function build configs: several ad-hoc paths for a
    job that has one.
  - deleted SUPABASE_KEYS_GUIDE.md and SUPABASE_KEYS_QUICK_ANSWER.md, which
    said the same thing twice and both published keys. Replaced by one
    docs/setup/supabase-keys.md: what the three values are, who may hold each,
    where each actually lives, and how to rotate — with no key material in it.
  - archived the two migration guides under docs/archive/ with the password
    replaced by $PGPASSWORD and a header saying plainly that what they named
    must be treated as compromised.
  - moved generate-supabase-keys.js into scripts/ (it generates random keys and
    leaks nothing; it was just loose). Deleted ga-check.tmp.mjs, a temp file
    from an earlier session.

Half two, the guard — src/secret-scan.test.ts. It scans every tracked text file
for credential VALUES rather than policing folders, which matters, because it
immediately found four leaks the root sweep would have missed entirely:

  docs/deploy/COOLIFY_EDGE_FUNCTIONS_SETUP.md   anon key, in full
  docs/deploy/SSL_MIGRATION_COMPLETE.md         anon key, in full
  docs/setup/AUTH_SETUP_DOCUMENTATION.md        anon key, in full, twice
                                                — and from a DIFFERENT
                                                  JWT_SECRET era than the first

Anon keys ship in the frontend bundle by design, so these are not severity-one
on their own. They are the same habit that published the service_role key, and
they will be dead the moment rotation happens. Redacted to their header segment.

Five rules: complete JWTs (three real segments — a truncated "eyJhbGci..." in
documentation still passes, deliberately), passwords assigned to literals,
connection strings with inline passwords, private key blocks with an actual
base64 body, and live third-party keys (Stripe, Supabase PAT, GitHub, OpenAI,
Anthropic, AWS, Slack).

It never prints a matched value — only file, line, rule and why. Reporting a
leak must not re-publish it.

FALSE POSITIVES, each judged and pinned. The first run produced 16 findings; 4
were real (above) and 12 were not. Rather than allowlist files wholesale I
narrowed the rules, and then pinned each exemption as its own assertion so that
widening one to smuggle a real secret past fails the test:
  - postgres:postgres@localhost — the throwaway verify-backend.yml runs. Exempt
    only because user equals password; a real password there still fails.
  - `Password: anything` / `Password: password` in QUICK_START.md — seeded demo
    accounts. Exact-match list of words-for-a-password, so `password_Xk92mQ`
    is not exempt.
  - $POSTGRES_PASSWORD, [password], ${...} — leading-sigil check.
  - google-indexing/index.ts stripping PEM headers with .replace(). The rule now
    requires base64 after the header: handling a key is not leaking one.
Two files are allowlisted outright, each with its reason: logger.test.ts, whose
fixture passwords exist to prove the logger redacts them, and tests/e2e/auth.spec.ts.

DEMONSTRATED ABLE TO FAIL, against the files as actually committed at 908a2c1,
not against a synthetic sample:
  SUPABASE_KEYS_GUIDE.md:82   complete JWT
  SUPABASE_KEYS_GUIDE.md:84   complete JWT
  deploy-migrations-ssh.ps1:11 password assigned to a literal
  deploy-migrations-ssh.ps1:13 password assigned to a literal

VERIFICATION: 76 test files, 654 tests, all passing — up from 75/647-with-2-red.
tsc --noEmit clean. eslint clean. prettier clean. CI needs no change: it already
runs npm run test:coverage, so the guard is enforced from the next push.

STILL OUTSTANDING, AND NOT SOMETHING THIS LOOP CAN DO:

  ROTATE. Removing a secret from the working tree does not remove it from git
  history, from clones, from forks, or from anyone who watched a public
  repository for five days. Treat as compromised: JWT_SECRET (which forces
  reissuing both anon and service_role), the Postgres superuser password, and
  the root SSH password on the production host. Procedure in
  docs/setup/supabase-keys.md.

  Scrubbing the history rewrites published commits. That is Dj's call, not this
  loop's, and rotation matters more than scrubbing either way.
